answers.question: How do the results compare with your predictions? Where were you furthest off? Use the numbers from your run, by number of articles.
answers.answer: In general, my predictions got the pattern right for the agent. 3 articles claims did best while 2 and 4 articles claims were lower (but I underestimated both by about 15%). I was furthest off for no tools. I think this is because when it answers "doesn't say", that matches "not supported" and half of the claims are "not supported". For one search, I expected it to drop as claims needed more articles, but it stayed the same (or even rose slightly). However, it got 0 of 50 "supported" claims right, so it seems it never confirmed a claim and was only right when it said "not supported".

answers.question: Does the gap between the agent and the one-search baseline grow with the number of articles? What in the claims or the traces explains what you see?
answers.answer: No, the gap between the agent and the one search baseline doesn't grow with the number of articles. It is biggest at 3 articles and smallest at 4. The one search stays almost flat because it is only right when it says "not supported" and that works the same however many articles a claim needs. So the gap is the claims the agent can confirm that one search can't. The agent was best at 3 articles and dropped at 4. For 4 articles, it needs to do more lookups, so it is more likely to wander off or run out.

answers.question: The no-tools baseline read nothing. How did it do, and what does that tell you about these claims?
answers.answer: The no tools baseline did better than I expected. But most of that comes from "not supported" claims. I think it usually can't recall the facts and answers "doesn't say" which matches "not supported". This tells me that means the overall score may not be a great measure and the "supported" row may show more about which one can actually check claims.
